The Art of
Waiting

How the wait became the product — and why being told no is the most powerful thing a brand can ever say to you

Leon Telemaque · 2026 · Consumer Psychology & Culture · Scarcity · Prestige · Manufactured Demand
A line for the 1970 Municipal Opera season — waiting as its own kind of advertisement

When the PS5 pre-orders dropped I was refreshing pages at two in the morning. Checking Twitter to see if anyone had spotted stock. Setting up alerts. Doing the kind of obsessive monitoring behaviour that in any other context would be a red flag about how you are spending your time. And the thing I remember most clearly is not the moment I finally got one. It is the feeling of watching someone else get one first. I expected that to deflate the desire a little. To take some of the edge off. It did the opposite. Seeing someone post their order confirmation made me want it more. I could not explain that at the time. I can now.

That experience was not unique to me and it was not unique to the PS5. It is a psychological mechanism that operates identically whether you are refreshing a retailer's website at midnight, waiting three years for a Hermès Birkin, trying to get a table at Rao's in New York, or sitting on a waitlist for a Wealthsimple credit card. The product changes completely. The psychology does not move at all. And once you see the mechanism clearly you start to understand that in many cases the wait is not a side effect of demand. The wait is the product itself.

I. Rao's Has Ten Tables

Rao's is a Southern Italian restaurant in East Harlem that has been operating since 1896. It has ten tables. The same regulars have been coming for decades and many of them have effectively inherited their reservations from family members. You cannot call and book a table. You cannot get on a waiting list in any conventional sense. If you do not already have a connection to someone who has a table at Rao's you are simply not going. That is the whole policy.

Rao's has ten tables and has been fully booked by the same regulars for decades. The impossibility of access is not a limitation. It is the entire value proposition.

The food is good. By all accounts it is genuinely good Italian American cooking. But there are hundreds of restaurants in New York serving genuinely good Italian American cooking and none of them are Rao's. None of them have the cultural weight, the celebrity clientele, the mythology, the status signal of having eaten there. Because you can get into all of them. Rao's you cannot. And that impossibility is what makes it one of the most famous restaurants in the world.

Frank Pellegrino who ran the restaurant for decades understood something that most restaurateurs never figure out. Expansion would have destroyed the thing that made Rao's valuable. More tables means more access. More access means less exclusivity. Less exclusivity means the regulars who come because nobody else can get in have no reason to keep coming. The ten tables are not a constraint on the business. They are the business model.

The scarcity is not the problem they never got around to solving. The scarcity is the decision they made on purpose and have been maintaining on purpose ever since.

II. The Birkin Was Never For Sale

Hermès introduced the Birkin bag in 1984 and it is now the most financially resilient luxury object ever created. The resale value of a Birkin consistently outperforms gold and the S&P 500 over any significant time period. There are Birkins that have appreciated 500% from their original retail price. And the reason for this is not the leather. It is not the craftsmanship, as exceptional as that craftsmanship is. It is the fact that you cannot simply decide you want a Birkin and go buy one.

The official process for acquiring a Birkin requires you to first establish a purchase history with Hermès. You need to have spent a significant amount of money on other Hermès products before a sales associate will even have a conversation with you about a Birkin. There is no price list. There is no order form. The bag is presented to you when Hermès decides you have earned the right to be offered one. The consumer who walks in off the street with $30,000 ready to spend cannot buy a Birkin. The consumer who has spent $30,000 over several years on scarves and belts and home goods might be offered one.

Hermès made the consumer audition for the right to spend their own money. And the consumer did it. Willingly. Happily. Gratefully.

What Hermès understood about consumer psychology is something that most brands never grasp. Desire is not a fixed quantity that exists before the purchase decision. Desire is produced by the process of trying to get the thing. The more difficult you make access the more the consumer invests psychologically in obtaining it. By the time a Hermès customer is offered a Birkin they have spent months or years cultivating a relationship with the brand. They have spent money they did not originally plan to spend. They have thought about the bag far more than they would have if they could have simply bought it on day one. The desire has compounded. The purchase when it finally happens feels like an achievement not a transaction.

III. Rolex Makes You Bring Six Witnesses

The Rolex waiting list is the most socially sophisticated version of this mechanism I have come across. Hermès makes you spend money with them first before they will consider offering you a Birkin. Rolex goes further than that. To purchase certain Rolex models at an authorised dealer you need to be referred by existing Rolex owners. Not one person. Six people. Six current owners of the brand have to vouch for you before you are even permitted to have the conversation about buying one.

Think about what that process requires of the consumer. You have to identify six people in your life who own a Rolex and are willing to put their name behind your desire to own one too. That means six conversations about the watch. Six people who now know you want one badly enough to ask them for a referral. Six people who are now tracking whether you eventually get it. Rolex turned their purchase qualification process into a word of mouth engine and made the consumer do all the work of running it.

Six referrals means six conversations about why you want a Rolex. Rolex did not run those conversations. You did. On their behalf. For free.

And the psychological effect on the buyer is extraordinary. By the time you have navigated six referrals and been approved to purchase, you have invested so much social capital in obtaining the watch that the purchase itself cannot possibly disappoint. You have told the story of wanting it so many times that the story has become part of your identity. The Rolex you eventually buy is not just a watch. It is the physical conclusion of a process that involved other people, took real time, and required you to publicly commit to wanting it. That is a level of pre-purchase psychological investment that most brands could never engineer even if they tried.

What makes the Rolex model different from the Birkin model is the social dimension. Hermès asks you to spend money to prove you belong. Rolex asks you to prove you belong socially. You need people who are already inside the community to vouch for you. That is a membership model disguised as a purchase process and it means that every Rolex owner is also a gatekeeper for the next one. The community polices its own exclusivity. Rolex does not have to do it themselves.

IV. The PS5 and What Watching Someone Else Get One Does To You

The PS5 launch in November 2020 was not managed as a scarcity play in the same deliberate way that Hermès manages the Birkin. The supply constraints were real. There were genuine semiconductor shortages, genuine logistics disruptions, genuine manufacturing limitations. Sony was not artificially restricting supply to manufacture prestige. But the effect on consumer psychology was identical to an intentional scarcity strategy and that is the interesting thing about it.

People were monitoring stock alerts around the clock. There were entire subreddits dedicated to tracking which retailers had inventory. Scalpers bought units in bulk and resold them at two and three times retail price and found a market of willing buyers. The PS5 became the most talked about consumer product of 2020 not because of its technical specifications but because of how hard it was to get. The difficulty of access was generating more cultural conversation than any marketing campaign Sony could have designed.

The part that stuck with me was what happened psychologically when you saw someone else get one. The rational response to seeing another person confirm their order would be some reduction in anxiety. The product exists. It is being delivered. Your turn will come. That is not what happened. Watching someone else get a day one PS5 while you were still waiting intensified the desire rather than easing it. The day one owner had something you did not have. Not just the console but the status of having been first. Of having navigated the chaos successfully. Of belonging to a group that was by definition limited in size. That status was part of the product and it was only available while other people were still waiting for it.

The people who got one first were not just early adopters. They were proof of concept. Living advertisements for a desire the rest of us already had and could not satisfy.

V. Wealthsimple Put 300,000 People on a List for a Free Credit Card

The Wealthsimple Cash card waitlist is the most interesting contemporary example of this mechanism because it applied a luxury psychology to a fintech product that was being offered at no cost. There was no Birkin price tag. There was no PS5 retail price. The card was free. And 300,000 people signed up to wait for it anyway.

Wealthsimple did not need a waitlist for operational reasons. They were not constrained by manufacturing capacity or semiconductor supply. They ran a waitlist because they understood that a product you have to wait for feels more valuable than a product you can have immediately. Being on the Wealthsimple waitlist positioned the card as something worth waiting for before anyone had experienced what the card actually did. The wait was doing marketing work that no campaign budget could replicate. Every person on the list was a person who had already made a psychological investment in a product they did not yet own.

And there was a social dimension to it. People posted about being on the waitlist. They told their friends. They checked their position in the queue. The waitlist turned passive consumers into active participants in the product's launch narrative. Wealthsimple got 300,000 people to do their marketing for them while simultaneously creating the impression that the card was so desirable that access to it had to be managed carefully. That is an extraordinary piece of consumer psychology executed with almost no budget.

VI. Supreme, Sneakers, and the Drop Model

Supreme codified the scarcity model for streetwear and in doing so changed how an entire generation of brands thinks about product releases. The Thursday drop. Limited quantities. No restocks. The line outside the Lafayette Street store that became a cultural event in itself. Supreme understood before almost anyone else in retail that the experience of trying to get the product was as valuable to the consumer as the product itself.

Nike absorbed this lesson and applied it to sneaker releases with the SNKRS app and the limited Jordan drops that followed. The SNKRS app is essentially a lottery with a shopping cart attached. You enter for the chance to buy. Most people who enter do not get access. The ones who do feel like they won something. The ones who do not want the shoe more next time. Nike manufactured a consumer psychology around footwear that had previously only existed around fine art and luxury collectibles. You are not buying a shoe. You are competing for the right to buy a shoe. And somehow that makes the shoe more desirable than it would have been if you could simply walk into a store and purchase it.

Supreme never restocks. Nike built an app that makes you enter a lottery to buy sneakers. The wait is not the obstacle to the purchase. The wait is the purchase experience itself.

VII. The Mechanism

What connects Rao's and the Birkin and the PS5 and the Wealthsimple waitlist and the Supreme drop is a single psychological principle that operates across all of them regardless of price point, product category, or industry. Scarcity does not just restrict access to a product. It transforms the meaning of the product. A thing you cannot have is a fundamentally different object psychologically than the same thing you can have whenever you want it.

There is a term in behavioural economics called reactance. When your freedom to obtain something is restricted your desire for that thing increases. This is not a bug in human psychology. It is a feature. It evolved for legitimate reasons. Resources that are scarce in nature are usually scarce because they are genuinely valuable and the psychological drive to obtain scarce things served real survival purposes. What brands have learned to do is trigger that same response in a completely manufactured context. The scarcity is not natural. It is designed. But the psychological reaction to it is exactly what it would be if the scarcity were real.

The Scarcity Mechanism — How It Works
  1. Access is restricted — by limited supply, a waitlist, a drop model, an invitation system, or a qualification process. The restriction can be real or manufactured. The psychology does not distinguish between them.
  2. Desire compounds during the wait — the consumer thinks about the product more than they would have if they could simply buy it. Psychological ownership begins before physical ownership. The product becomes more valuable in the mind the longer access is denied.
  3. Social proof intensifies the effect — watching others get access while you are still waiting does not reduce desire. It increases it. The day one owner is proof that the thing is real and obtainable. They are also evidence that you have not yet obtained it.
  4. Access feels like achievement — when the consumer finally gets the product the transaction feels like a reward for patience and persistence rather than a simple purchase. The emotional weight of the acquisition is dramatically higher than it would have been for an immediately available product.
  5. Ownership carries status — the consumer who succeeded in obtaining the scarce thing has a story to tell and a signal to send. Day one PS5 owner. Birkin holder. Rao's regular. The ownership is social currency in a way that an immediately available product can never be.

The most important thing to understand about this mechanism is that it does not require the product to be objectively superior to create the psychological effect. The Birkin is beautifully made but there are other bags made with comparable craftsmanship that you can buy tomorrow. The PS5 is a powerful console but so is the Xbox Series X which was available at launch. Rao's serves excellent Italian food but so do dozens of other restaurants in New York that you can actually get into. The scarcity is doing work that the product itself cannot do and in many cases does not need to do.

What I find genuinely fascinating about this is that most consumers understand it on some level and it does not matter. I knew while I was refreshing those stock pages at two in the morning that Sony's supply constraints were partly a function of circumstances beyond their control and partly a function of a launch strategy that benefits from high visible demand and low immediate availability. Knowing that did not reduce the desire at all. The psychology operates below the level where rational awareness can intercept it. You can understand the mechanism completely and still feel its full effect. That is what makes it such a durable tool for the brands that use it well.

The wait is not a problem to be solved. It is a product to be designed. And the brands that understand that are selling you something you never see on the receipt.
